# A tour of the standard library

A good language without a library is exhausting. Nim ships its standard library with the compiler,
and its modules are imported with the `std/` prefix. This chapter tours the four modules you reach
for most days: `strutils`, `sequtils`, `tables`, and `json`. Each gets enough coverage to be
useful; the rest have their own chapters.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can process text with `std/strutils`, transform sequences with
`std/sequtils`, store keyed values in a `Table`, read and build JSON, and choose between `Table`
and `seq` with a clear reason.
:::

## Importing standard library modules

Standard library modules are imported with the `std/` prefix, for example `import std/strutils` or
`import std/sequtils`. The prefix separates official modules from local files. Without the import,
names such as `strip` or `hasKey` are unknown to the compiler.

## `std/strutils`: working with text

```{.nim}
import std/strutils

let line = "  Ada,36,London  "

echo line.strip
echo line.strip.split(',')
echo "ada".toUpperAscii
echo "hello".startsWith("he")
echo @["a", "b", "c"].join("-")
```

```{.txt}
Ada,36,London
@["Ada", "36", "London"]
ADA
true
a-b-c
```

`strip` removes spaces from both ends. `split(',')` breaks a string into a `seq[string]`.
`toUpperAscii` uppercases letters, and `startsWith` tests a prefix. `join("-")` joins a
`seq[string]` back into one string with a separator. All of these return new values; the original
string is untouched.

## `std/sequtils`: transforming sequences

```{.nim}
import std/sequtils

let numbers = @[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

echo numbers.filterIt(it mod 2 == 0)
echo numbers.mapIt(it * it)
echo numbers.filterIt(it > 2).mapIt(it * 10)
```

```{.txt}
@[2, 4, 6]
@[1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36]
@[30, 40, 50, 60]
```

`filterIt` keeps matching elements, `mapIt` transforms each element. Both are templates: inside the
parentheses, `it` refers to the element being processed. Both return a new `seq` and can be chained,
as on the last line.

## `std/tables`: mapping keys to values

```{.nim}
import std/tables

var ages = initTable[string, int]()
ages["ada"] = 36
ages["grace"] = 45

echo ages["ada"]
echo ages.hasKey("linus")
echo ages.getOrDefault("linus", -1)
echo ages.len
```

```{.txt}
36
false
-1
2
```

`Table[string, int]` maps `string` keys to `int` values. `initTable` creates an empty table;
writing `ages["ada"] = 36` adds a new pair. `hasKey` tests whether a key exists, and
`getOrDefault` returns a default value when the key is missing. This is far handier than scanning
a `seq` one item at a time.

## `Table` or `seq`?

Both store many values, but for different needs.

| Need | Choice |
|---|---|
| order matters, access by index | `seq` |
| fast lookup by key | `Table` |
| small data read in order | `seq` |

A `Table` stores through a hash function, so lookups are nearly instant no matter how much it
holds. A `seq` must be checked one by one, but its order is fixed and elements are reached by
index. For small data the choice often falls to `seq` for its simplicity.

## `std/json`: reading data

```{.nim}
import std/json

let doc = """{"name": "Ada", "age": 36, "tags": ["math", "code"]}"""
let data = parseJson(doc)

echo data["name"].getStr
echo data["age"].getInt
echo data["tags"][1].getStr
echo data.pretty
```

```{.txt}
Ada
36
code
{
  "name": "Ada",
  "age": 36,
  "tags": [
    "math",
    "code"
  ]
}
```

`parseJson` turns JSON text into a `JsonNode`. Fields are reached like a map: `data["name"]`. To
pull out the value, use `getStr`, `getInt`, `getFloat`, or `getBool` to match its kind. `pretty`
prints JSON with indentation so it is easy to read.

## `std/json`: building data

```{.nim}
import std/json

let person = %*{
  "name": "Ada",
  "age": 36,
  "tags": ["math", "code"]
}

echo person.pretty

type Person = object
  name: string
  age: int

let parsed = person.to(Person)
echo parsed.name, " is ", parsed.age
```

```{.txt}
{
  "name": "Ada",
  "age": 36,
  "tags": [
    "math",
    "code"
  ]
}
Ada is 36
```

`%*{...}` builds a `JsonNode` straight from a literal, without writing a JSON string and parsing it
back. `to(Type)` turns it into an ordinary object. Both avoid error-prone manual string assembly.

## Reading an error: a missing key

Reaching for a missing key is not a compile error; the program only stops while running.

```{.nim}
import std/json

let data = """{"age": 36}""".parseJson
echo data["name"]
```

```{.txt}
Error: unhandled exception: key not found: name [KeyError]
```

The message names the missing key and the `KeyError` kind. The full output also carries a stack
trace. Test with `hasKey` before reading, or use `getOrDefault`, so the program does not stop when
the key is gone.

## Other modules have their own chapters

The standard library is far larger than these four modules. `std/os` is covered in the files and
operating system chapter, `std/strformat` in the variables chapter, and `std/math` and
`std/algorithm` appear in the operators and files chapters. `std/random` and `std/times` are covered in the
[time and random](times-and-random.qmd) chapter. The import pattern is
always the same: `import std/name`.

## Exercises

1. Read a sentence, split it, uppercase each word with `toUpperAscii`, then join them back with
   `join("-")`.
2. Without running it, predict the output:
   ```{.nim}
   import std/sequtils

   let xs = @[3, 1, 2]
   echo xs.filterIt(it > 1).mapIt(it * 2)
   ```
3. Create a `Table[string, int]` with three values, print one existing value, and one value through
   `getOrDefault` for a missing key.
4. Write from scratch: parse `{"city": "Bandung"}` and print the value of `city`.
5. The code below fails while running. Fix it without changing the contents of `t`, then explain
   the error message:
   ```{.nim}
   import std/tables

   let t = {"a": 1}.toTable
   echo t["b"]
   ```

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

## Summary

- Standard library modules are imported with the `std/` prefix, for example `import std/strutils`.
- `strutils` processes text (`strip`, `split`, `join`), `sequtils` transforms sequences
  (`filterIt`, `mapIt`).
- `Table[K, V]` maps keys to values for fast lookup; `seq` remains the choice when order matters.
- `parseJson` and `%*` read and build JSON; `to`, `getInt`, and `pretty` complete the set.
- A missing key raises `KeyError` while running, so test with `hasKey` first.
